prompt:
Plan how to add a "Download CSV" button to the monthly sales report page. Users currently only
see the report as an HTML table. Describe the steps, the files to change and how you would test it.
context:
Flask app. `reports/views.py` has `monthly_report()` which builds a list of row dicts and renders
`templates/monthly.html`. Reports can have up to 200,000 rows. Customer names can contain commas,
quotes and non-ASCII characters. Only users with the `finance` role may open reports.

required_points.text: Reuses the existing row-building logic in one place instead of duplicating the query
Adds an endpoint (or format parameter) that returns text/csv with a Content-Disposition filename
Streams the response so 200,000 rows do not have to fit in memory
Uses a CSV library to escape commas, quotes and newlines and writes UTF-8 (optionally with a BOM for Excel)
Applies the same authorisation (finance role) to the new endpoint
Guards against CSV/formula injection in cells that start with =, +, - or @
Adds tests for escaping, headers, permissions and a large export

forbidden_points.text: Builds the whole CSV as one string by concatenation in memory with no escaping

prompt:
Plan the implementation of a "forgot password" flow (email a reset link) for our web app, which
currently has login with email and password only.
context:
Node.js with Express and PostgreSQL. Users are in a `users` table (`id`, `email`, `password_hash`
using bcrypt). Email is sent through a helper `lib/mailer.ts` (SendGrid). There is no existing
token or reset table. About 30,000 users.

required_points.text: Generates a cryptographically random, single-use, expiring token and stores only a hash of it
Adds a table or columns for reset tokens with an expiry and used timestamp (migration)
Avoids user enumeration: the same response whether or not the email exists
Rate-limits reset requests per account and IP
On reset, validates the token, sets a new bcrypt hash, invalidates the token and existing sessions
Sends the link over HTTPS from a configured base URL and does not log the token
Adds tests for expiry, reuse and unknown email

forbidden_points.text: Emails the user's current or a newly generated password in plaintext
keywords: send the new password in the email

prompt:
Plan adding a dark mode to our React web app, including remembering the user's choice. Cover
what to change and how to verify it.
context:
React 18 with TypeScript, styled with a single global `styles/app.css` that uses hard-coded hex
colours in about 400 rules, plus a handful of inline styles in `components/Chart.tsx`. Users are
logged in; preferences are not yet stored on the server.

required_points.text: Introduces CSS custom properties (design tokens) for colours and replaces hard-coded values
Defines a dark palette and switches it with a data attribute or class on the root element
Respects the operating-system preference by default and lets the user override it
Persists the choice (localStorage, cookie or user profile) and applies it before first paint to avoid a flash
Handles the places CSS cannot reach: inline styles, chart colours and images/logos
Checks contrast and accessibility in both themes and tests visually

forbidden_points.text: Duplicates the whole stylesheet as a second hard-coded copy for dark mode

prompt:
The `GET /api/invoices` endpoint returns every invoice for a customer in one response and some
customers now have 50,000 of them. Plan the change to add pagination without breaking existing clients.
context:
Python FastAPI service, PostgreSQL, `invoices` table with `id` (UUID), `customer_id`, `created_at`.
Two internal clients (a web app and a mobile app) call the endpoint; the mobile app updates
slowly. Results are sorted by `created_at` descending.

required_points.text: Chooses cursor (keyset) pagination, or justifies offset pagination, and defines the response shape (items, next cursor)
Uses a stable sort with a tie-breaker (created_at plus id) and an index that supports it
Keeps old clients working: default page size or opt-in parameter, versioning, or a deprecation period
Sets a sensible default and maximum page size and validates parameters
Updates the web and mobile clients and documentation (OpenAPI)
Tests boundaries: empty result, exactly one page, rows inserted during paging, invalid cursor

forbidden_points.text: Loads all rows and slices them in application memory

prompt:
Plan adding structured logging with a request id to our API service so that support can follow
one request through the logs. Today the code uses scattered `print` and `logging.info` calls
with free-form strings.
context:
Python/Flask service with about 60 endpoints, deployed as 4 containers, logs shipped to a
central log store that can parse JSON. A second internal service is called over HTTP from some
handlers.

required_points.text: Configures one logging setup that emits JSON (timestamp, level, message, logger, request id)
Generates or accepts an incoming request id in middleware and attaches it to every log line (contextvars or logging filter)
Propagates the request id to downstream HTTP calls and returns it in a response header
Replaces print and ad-hoc strings incrementally, with a lint or review rule to stop regressions
Keeps secrets and personal data out of logs (redaction)
Verifies in tests and with a sample query in the log store, and sets log levels per environment

forbidden_points.text: Logs full request and response bodies, including credentials, at INFO

prompt:
Plan an admin audit log: a record of who changed what in the app (user roles, pricing rules,
feature settings), viewable by administrators.
context:
Django monolith with about 12 models, PostgreSQL, Django admin plus a custom React admin that
calls DRF endpoints. Changes can come from the API, the Django admin and management commands.
Auditors ask for records to be kept for 2 years.

required_points.text: Defines what is recorded: actor, timestamp, action, object type and id, and before/after values
Captures changes at a single choke point (model signals, a mixin, or a library such as django-simple-history) so no path is missed
Records the actor for API, admin and management-command changes (including system actors)
Stores entries append-only in their own table with indexes for browsing and keeps them for the required retention
Adds a read-only admin view with filtering and pagination, restricted to administrators
Excludes secrets such as password hashes from recorded values
Tests that each entry point writes an entry

forbidden_points.text: Relies on application logs as the audit trail
keywords: the logs are the audit trail

prompt:
Plan search-as-you-type for the customer list in our admin UI. Today the page loads all
customers (about 25,000) and filters them in the browser, which is slow to open.
context:
React front-end, Go backend with PostgreSQL. `GET /api/customers` returns everything. Staff search
by name, email or company, often with typos or partial words.

required_points.text: Moves search to the server with a query parameter and a limited result set
Debounces input and cancels or ignores stale in-flight requests
Adds database support for partial and fuzzy matches (pg_trgm or an ILIKE with an index)
Handles loading, empty and error states and keyboard accessibility
Sets a minimum query length and a maximum result count, and escapes wildcard characters
Tests the endpoint and the component, including rapid typing

forbidden_points.text: Keeps loading all customers to the browser and only optimises the filter loop

prompt:
Our service drops in-flight requests during Kubernetes deploys, and the load balancer
sometimes sends traffic to pods that are still starting. Plan the changes to fix both.
context:
A Go HTTP service on Kubernetes (3 replicas, rolling updates). It connects to PostgreSQL and
Redis at startup and takes up to 20 seconds to warm a cache. The Deployment has no probes today.

required_points.text: Adds a readiness endpoint that reports ready only after dependencies and warm-up are done
Adds a liveness probe that is cheap and does not depend on external services
Handles SIGTERM with graceful shutdown (stop accepting, drain in-flight requests with a deadline)
Coordinates with Kubernetes: terminationGracePeriodSeconds, a preStop sleep or readiness flip, and rolling-update settings
Adds a startup probe or initial delay for the slow warm-up
Verifies by deploying under load and watching error rates

forbidden_points.text: Makes the liveness probe check the database so that a database outage restarts every pod
keywords: liveness probe should check the database
restart pods when the database is down

prompt:
Plan adding optional TOTP two-factor authentication (authenticator apps) to our web app, with
recovery codes.
context:
Rails app with Devise, PostgreSQL. 80,000 users, some are admins who should eventually be
required to use 2FA. The app also has an API authenticated with personal access tokens.

required_points.text: Adds secret storage (encrypted at rest) and enrolment with a QR code and confirmation of a first valid code
Verifies TOTP codes with a small time window, prevents code reuse and rate-limits attempts
Generates single-use recovery codes, stored hashed, and a regeneration flow
Integrates with login (second step after the password) and with session handling
Decides how API tokens and other login paths (SSO, remember-me) interact with 2FA
Plans a safe disable and lost-device process, with identity verification
Plans rollout (opt-in, then required for admins), migration and tests

forbidden_points.text: Stores the TOTP secret in plaintext or logs codes

prompt:
Our app has a single boolean `is_admin` on users. Product wants roles (viewer, editor, billing,
admin) with permissions per project. Plan the move to role-based access control.
context:
Spring Boot (Java 17) with PostgreSQL and a React front-end. Authorisation is currently done with
`if (user.isAdmin())` checks in about 140 places across controllers and services. Roles apply
per project; a user can have different roles in different projects.

required_points.text: Models roles, permissions and per-project role assignments in the database with a migration
Centralises permission checks in one policy layer instead of scattering conditionals
Inventories the existing 140 `isAdmin` checks and migrates them gradually, mapping each to a permission
Maps existing admins to the admin role and keeps behaviour identical at cutover (data migration, compatibility shim)
Enforces the same rules on the server for the API, and uses the front-end only for hiding UI
Tests the permission matrix, including cross-project access and privilege escalation
Adds an audit trail for role changes

forbidden_points.text: Hides forbidden actions only in the UI without server-side checks

prompt:
Our web app polls `/api/notifications` every five seconds from 20,000 open tabs, which loads
the API and the database. Plan the move to server-sent events (SSE) for notifications.
context:
Node.js API on three instances behind an nginx load balancer, PostgreSQL, Redis. Notifications are
created by several services. Browsers must keep working behind corporate proxies and mobile
networks; missed notifications are not acceptable.

required_points.text: Adds an SSE endpoint with authentication, correct headers and heartbeats to keep connections alive
Uses Redis pub/sub (or similar) so that events reach the instance that holds the user's connection
Supports resuming after reconnect with Last-Event-ID and server-side storage of recent events, so none are missed
Configures nginx and proxies for long-lived streaming connections (buffering off, timeouts)
Keeps a polling fallback and rolls out gradually with a flag
Plans capacity (connections per instance, file descriptors) and verifies with a load test

forbidden_points.text: Removes polling for all users in one release with no fallback

prompt: Plan adding multi-currency pricing (USD, EUR, GBP) to our shop, which has only ever sold in USD.
context:
Django shop with PostgreSQL. `Product.price` is a DecimalField in USD; orders store `total`
in USD; payments go through Stripe. Finance exports monthly reports in USD. Roughly 5% of
traffic is from Europe and the UK.

required_points.text: Decides how prices are stored (explicit per-currency prices vs conversion) and stores money as integer minor units or fixed decimals with a currency code
Defines where exchange rates come from and when they are locked (at order time) if conversion is used
Stores the currency and the amounts on orders and payments so that history stays correct
Handles rounding and display per currency (decimal places, formatting, tax-inclusive pricing)
Updates Stripe usage (currency per charge, refunds in the original currency)
Updates reporting for finance (per currency and converted totals) and migrates existing data
Rolls out gradually with tests around cart, checkout and refunds

forbidden_points.text: Stores prices as floating-point numbers

prompt:
Plan adding per-user API keys with rate limits so that customers can call our API from their
own scripts. Today the API only accepts browser sessions.
context:
FastAPI service with PostgreSQL and Redis, 5,000 active customers, three plans with different
request limits. Keys must be revocable, and customers must be able to see when a key was last used.

required_points.text: Generates high-entropy keys shown once, with a prefix for identification, and stores only a hash
Adds a keys table with owner, name, scopes, created, last used and revoked columns
Authenticates keys in middleware or a dependency, with scope checks and constant-time comparison
Enforces per-plan rate limits (Redis counters) and returns 429 with headers
Provides self-service UI or endpoints to create, list and revoke keys with immediate effect
Handles last-used tracking without a database write per request, and monitors abuse
Documents and tests the feature (including leaked-key guidance)

forbidden_points.text: Stores the keys in plaintext so support can read them back
keywords: so support can look up the key

prompt:
Our schema is managed by hand: engineers paste SQL into production from a wiki page. Plan the
introduction of a proper migration tool without disrupting current work.
context:
A Node.js service with PostgreSQL in three environments (dev, staging, production). There is a
`schema.sql` that is often out of date. 8 engineers, deploys several times a day through
GitHub Actions.

required_points.text: Picks a migration tool (Flyway, Liquibase, Knex, Prisma Migrate, Alembic or similar) with stated criteria
Creates a baseline migration from the actual production schema and verifies that all environments match it
Runs migrations automatically in CI/CD before the app deploy, with locking against concurrent runs
Defines rules for safe migrations (backward compatible, no long locks, expand/contract) and review
Plans rollback or roll-forward strategy and backups before risky changes
Retires the manual process (wiki, direct production access) and communicates the change

forbidden_points.text: Regenerates the production schema from an ORM synchronise mode on startup

prompt:
Plan adding file attachments (PDF, images, up to 25 MB) to support tickets, visible to the
customer and to agents.
context:
Ruby on Rails app on AWS, PostgreSQL, S3 available. Tickets belong to organisations; agents see
all tickets, customers only their own organisation's. Some customers are in regulated industries.

required_points.text: Stores files in private object storage (not the app server or database) with direct or proxied upload and a size limit
Validates type and size on the server (content sniffing, allow-list), not just by extension
Scans uploads for malware and holds them until clean
Authorises downloads per ticket and organisation using short-lived signed URLs or an authenticated proxy
Serves files safely (Content-Disposition attachment, nosniff, separate domain) to prevent stored XSS
Plans retention, deletion with the ticket, and backups or encryption for regulated customers
Adds tests and UI states for upload progress, errors and rejection

forbidden_points.text: Saves uploads into a public web directory under the user's original file name
keywords: save them in the public folder
keep the original filename in the public directory

prompt:
Plan implementing soft delete with restore for projects, tasks and comments, replacing the
current hard deletes. Users have asked for an "undo" and a trash view.
context:
Laravel (PHP 8) app with MySQL, about 25 tables related by foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE.
There is a nightly report that counts tasks and a unique index on `projects(slug)`. A privacy
policy promises permanent deletion within 30 days of a user's request.

required_points.text: Adds a `deleted_at` column (or equivalent) and applies it with a model-level scope so deleted rows are hidden by default
Handles cascades explicitly: deleting a project hides its tasks and comments, and restoring brings back the right ones
Fixes unique constraints and reports that soft-deleted rows would break (slug reuse, counts, joins)
Adds a trash view and restore action with permissions
Adds a purge job that permanently deletes after a retention period, honouring the 30-day privacy promise
Migrates safely (backfill, no long table locks) and tests restore and cascade behaviour

forbidden_points.text: Keeps soft-deleted personal data forever

prompt:
Plan internationalising our React app so it can ship in English, German and Japanese. It is
English-only today with strings written directly in components.
context:
React 18 + TypeScript, about 300 components, dates and prices formatted with ad-hoc
`toFixed(2)` and `toLocaleDateString()`. Some strings are built by concatenation
("You have " + n + " items"). The backend returns some user-facing error messages in English.

required_points.text: Chooses an i18n library (react-intl, i18next or similar) and a message-catalog format with keys and pluralisation
Extracts hard-coded strings incrementally, with tooling to find them and a lint rule to stop new ones
Replaces string concatenation with parameterised, pluralised messages (word order differs by language)
Uses Intl APIs for dates, numbers and currencies instead of manual formatting
Handles locale detection, persistence and fallback, plus backend error messages (codes instead of text)
Sets up the translation workflow (translators, platform, review) and layout/font checks for Japanese and long German text

forbidden_points.text: Translates by building strings with concatenation in each language

prompt:
Plan scheduled and recurring reports: users pick a saved report, a schedule (daily, weekly,
monthly) and recipients, and receive it by email as a PDF.
context:
Django app on Kubernetes (4 replicas), PostgreSQL, Celery with Redis for background tasks. A
`SavedReport` model exists and PDF generation (`render_pdf(report)`) takes 5 to 60 seconds.
Users are in many time zones.

required_points.text: Models schedules (cron-like rule, time zone, recipients, enabled, last/next run) and stores the time zone with the schedule
Runs a single scheduler that enqueues due runs (Celery beat or a poller), avoiding duplicate runs across replicas
Executes each report as an idempotent background task with retries, timeouts and failure notification
Handles daylight-saving transitions and missed runs after downtime (catch-up policy)
Controls email delivery: recipient validation, attachment size limits, links instead of attachments for large files, unsubscribe
Applies permissions at run time (the owner's access), and limits schedules per user to protect capacity
Adds a UI to manage schedules and a run history, plus tests with a frozen clock

forbidden_points.text: Runs a cron entry on every replica without coordination
keywords: run the scheduler in each replica

prompt:
Plan moving our monolith's authentication from its own username/password table to an external
OpenID Connect identity provider (SSO) for enterprise customers, while the existing 60,000
users keep working.
context:
Java Spring monolith with PostgreSQL. Users log in with email and password (bcrypt). Sessions
are server-side. A few enterprise customers want SAML/OIDC with their own IdP and automatic
deprovisioning. Some integrations use long-lived API tokens issued to users.

required_points.text: Separates identity from the user record and links external identities (issuer and subject) to existing users with a migration
Implements the OIDC authorisation-code flow with PKCE and validates tokens (signature, issuer, audience, nonce, expiry)
Defines account linking and matching rules safely (verified email, no automatic takeover of existing accounts)
Supports per-tenant IdP configuration and just-in-time provisioning with role mapping
Handles deprovisioning and session lifetime (SCIM or back-channel logout, short sessions, re-check)
Keeps password login working during the transition, with enforced SSO per tenant later, and a break-glass admin path
Addresses API tokens issued to users (bind to identity state, migration plan) and tests with a staging IdP

forbidden_points.text: Trusts the email claim from any IdP to log into an existing account without verification
keywords: log in by email match from any provider

prompt:
Plan replacing our homegrown, database-backed job queue (about 3 million jobs a day) with a
managed queue service, without losing or double-running jobs during the cutover.
context:
Python workers poll a `jobs` table with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. Jobs include payment
captures that must run exactly once in effect. 25 job types, some scheduled for the future,
some with priorities. The team can accept a few minutes of added latency but not data loss.

required_points.text: Inventories job types and their semantics (idempotency, ordering, scheduling, priority, max runtime) and maps them onto the new service's features
Makes handlers idempotent (idempotency keys, effect-level dedupe) before moving, since the new queue is at-least-once
Uses a dual-publish or outbox-based migration with per-job-type cutover, rather than a big-bang switch
Drains the old queue, handles in-flight and scheduled jobs, and defines how to prevent double execution at the boundary
Plans monitoring (depth, age, failures, dead-letter) and comparison of old vs new throughput and results during the migration
Defines a rollback path and a reconciliation check for lost jobs
Plans cost, limits (message size, visibility timeout, rate limits) and decommissioning the old table

forbidden_points.text: Switches all producers and workers to the new queue in one deploy with no fallback
keywords: flip all job types in one release

prompt:
Plan extracting billing (invoices, subscriptions, payments) from our Rails monolith into its
own service, without stopping feature work or breaking invoicing at month end.

required_points.text: Maps the existing coupling (tables, joins, callbacks, shared models) before choosing the boundary
Introduces the boundary inside the monolith first (module, interface, anti-corruption layer) and removes direct table access incrementally
Plans the data move: new database, migration, replication or dual-write period, with verification and a cutover
Addresses consistency across the new boundary (events, outbox, idempotency, eventual consistency for reads)
Schedules around month-end close and has rollback or freeze rules
Plans team ownership, API contracts and contract tests, and observability of the new service
Treats the extraction as staged milestones with measurable exit criteria

forbidden_points.text: Proposes a rewrite of billing from scratch behind a big-bang switch
keywords: stop feature work for the rewrite

prompt:
Plan adding usage-based billing: customers are charged per API call above a free tier, billed
monthly. Today every customer pays a flat subscription.
context:
The API handles about 5,000 requests per second across regions. Billing uses Stripe
subscriptions. Disputes will happen, so every invoice line must be explainable, and customers
want a live usage page. Request logs exist but are sampled.

required_points.text: Defines the billable event precisely (what counts, per customer, with a unique id) and records usage in a dedicated, durable metering pipeline, not from sampled logs
Makes metering idempotent and tolerant of duplicates, late arrival and replays (dedupe keys, event time)
Aggregates usage per period with a reproducible computation and reconciles it against raw events
Integrates with Stripe metered billing or usage records, with free tier, proration and invoice line detail
Provides customers a usage page and alerts or spend caps, plus an explanation path for disputes
Handles scale and failure: buffering at the edge, regional aggregation, backfill after outages
Plans rollout in shadow mode (compute but do not charge) and compares with expectations before enabling

forbidden_points.text: Derives billable usage from sampled access logs
keywords: use the sampled logs for billing
estimate usage from the access log sample

prompt:
Plan the upgrade of our Django project from 3.2 (end of life) to the current release, without
freezing feature development.
context:
A 400,000-line codebase, 1,800 tests that take 35 minutes, about 70 third-party dependencies of
which a dozen are unmaintained, custom middleware and a custom user model. Deploys happen daily.
Python is 3.8 today.

required_points.text: Upgrades in steps through each intermediate release (and the supported Python versions) rather than a single jump
Starts with inventory and safety nets: dependency audit, test coverage gaps, deprecation warnings as errors
Handles unmaintained dependencies explicitly (replace, fork or vendor) and tracks them
Upgrades Python in a separate step and runs CI against both old and new versions during the transition
Keeps feature work flowing: small mergeable PRs, a long-lived branch avoided, compatibility shims
Plans deployment safety: canary or staged rollout, rollback, database migration review, performance and memory checks
Speeds up the test suite or parallelises it to shorten the feedback loop

forbidden_points.text: Upgrades straight from 3.2 to the newest release in one change
keywords: jump straight to the latest version in one pr

prompt:
Our primary PostgreSQL instance is at 80% CPU, mostly from read queries. Plan introducing read
replicas and routing reads to them without showing users stale or inconsistent data.
context:
A Go service using `database/sql` with a single connection pool. About 85% of queries are reads,
but some read-after-write paths exist (a user saves a setting and the next page shows it).
Managed PostgreSQL with streaming replicas available in the same region. Replica lag is
usually under 100 ms but spikes to seconds during batch jobs.

required_points.text: Adds a second pool for replicas and an explicit way to choose it (read-only transaction or repository method), defaulting to the primary
Identifies read-after-write paths and keeps them on the primary or uses session stickiness for a short time
Monitors replica lag and falls back to the primary when lag exceeds a threshold
Classifies queries and migrates them gradually, starting with safe heavy reads (reports, search, lists)
Handles failures: replica unavailable, failover, connection limits and pool sizing
Considers cheaper options in parallel (indexes, query tuning, caching) and measures the effect
Tests consistency behaviour and rolls out behind a flag with dashboards

forbidden_points.text: Sends every read to the replicas, including those that follow a write
keywords: send all reads to the replica

prompt:
Plan data retention and archival for our 2 TB `events` table, which grows by 60 GB a month and
is slowing queries and backups. Product only needs the last 90 days online; compliance requires
the data for 7 years.
context:
PostgreSQL 14 on managed cloud, a single non-partitioned table with a primary key on `id` and
indexes on `(account_id, created_at)` and `type`. A reporting job reads up to a year back.
Writes are continuous, about 200 per second.

required_points.text: Converts to time-based partitioning (by month or week) and explains how to migrate a live 2 TB table without long locks
Detaches or drops old partitions instead of running giant deletes, and archives them first to cheap storage in an open format
Meets the 7-year compliance requirement: archive integrity, retrievability and a tested restore or query path
Adapts the queries and the reporting job (partition pruning, queries beyond 90 days use the archive)
Automates the lifecycle (create future partitions, detach and archive old ones) with monitoring and alerts
Handles backups, indexes and storage reclaim (smaller backups, per-partition indexes) and verifies the migration with checks
Plans a staged rollout with a rollback plan and a rehearsal on a copy

forbidden_points.text: Deletes years of rows with one long DELETE statement on the live table
keywords: run a delete from events where
delete the old rows in one statement
